Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 1) The normal fasting plasma glucose level is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: A fasting plasma glucose of 70–99 mg/dL is considered normal in healthy adults.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 2) Diabetes mellitus is diagnosed when fasting plasma glucose is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: A fasting plasma glucose of ≥126 mg/dL on two separate occasions is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 3) An HbA1c value diagnostic of diabetes mellitus is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher is one of the accepted diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 4) Which investigation best reflects average blood glucose over the preceding 2–3 months?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: HbA1c reflects long-term glycemic control because it depends on the lifespan of red blood cells.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 5) The oral glucose tolerance test is most useful in diagnosing:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: The OGTT is particularly useful when fasting glucose is inconclusive or impaired glucose tolerance is suspected.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 6) The principal hormone responsible for lowering blood glucose is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Insulin is the only hormone that decreases blood glucose by promoting cellular glucose uptake and storage.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 7) Insulin is secreted by:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: β-cells of the pancreatic islets synthesize and secrete insulin.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 8) Glucagon is secreted by:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Glucagon is produced by pancreatic α-cells and increases blood glucose levels.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 9) Which hormone inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Somatostatin, secreted by δ-cells, suppresses the release of several gastrointestinal and pancreatic hormones.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 10) The principal action of glucagon is to:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 11) Type 1 diabetes mellitus is primarily caused by:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells leads to absolute insulin deficiency.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 12) The major pathogenic mechanism in type 2 diabetes mellitus is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Type 2 diabetes is characterized mainly by insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 13) Which acute complication is more characteristic of type 1 diabetes mellitus?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Absolute insulin deficiency promotes lipolysis and ketone body formation, leading to diabetic ketoacidosis.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 14) The principal ketone body responsible for metabolic acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: β-Hydroxybutyrate is the predominant ketone body contributing to acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 15) Microalbuminuria is an early marker of:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Persistent microalbuminuria is the earliest clinically detectable sign of diabetic kidney disease.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 16) The major protein responsible for maintaining plasma oncotic pressure is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and is the primary determinant of colloid osmotic pressure.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 17) Albumin is synthesized in the:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Hepatocytes synthesize albumin, which transports many endogenous and exogenous substances.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 18) The most abundant plasma protein is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Albumin accounts for approximately 60% of total plasma protein.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 19) A marked rise in serum ALT is most suggestive of:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: ALT is relatively specific for hepatocellular damage and rises markedly in acute hepatitis.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 20) Which enzyme is most specific for hepatocellular injury?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: ALT is more liver-specific than AST and is a sensitive indicator of hepatocyte injury.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 21) A marked elevation of alkaline phosphatase is most suggestive of:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: ALP rises significantly in biliary obstruction and cholestatic disorders.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 22) Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) is particularly useful in confirming that an elevated ALP is of:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: A raised GGT with elevated ALP supports a hepatobiliary source rather than bone disease.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 23) The principal pigment responsible for jaundice is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Jaundice results from increased bilirubin deposition in tissues.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 24) Unconjugated bilirubin is transported in plasma mainly bound to:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble and circulates tightly bound to albumin.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 25) A patient with obstructive jaundice is most likely to have:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Obstruction of bile flow causes reflux of conjugated bilirubin into the bloodstream and is typically associated with elevated ALP and GGT.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 26) The enzyme responsible for conjugation of bilirubin in the liver is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: This enzyme converts unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble conjugated bilirubin for biliary excretion.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 27) The major nitrogenous end product measured to assess renal function is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Serum creatinine is a reliable indicator of glomerular filtration rate and renal function.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 28) Blood urea is primarily synthesized in the:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Urea is produced in the liver through the urea cycle and excreted by the kidneys.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 29) The best routine biochemical marker of glomerular filtration rate is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Serum creatinine is widely used to estimate glomerular filtration rate in clinical practice.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 30) Hyperuricemia is the biochemical hallmark of:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Elevated serum uric acid leads to monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 31) The enzyme most commonly used in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Serum lipase is more sensitive and remains elevated longer than amylase in acute pancreatitis.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 32) Which enzyme rises earliest after acute pancreatitis?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Serum amylase usually rises within a few hours of the onset of acute pancreatitis.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 33) The principal hormone secreted by the thyroid gland is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: The thyroid gland secretes predominantly thyroxine (T₄), which is converted to the more active T₃ in peripheral tissues.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 34) Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is secreted by the:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: TSH stimulates thyroid hormone synthesis and release from the thyroid gland.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 35) The most sensitive initial investigation for suspected primary hypothyroidism is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Serum TSH is the most sensitive screening test for primary thyroid dysfunction.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 36) Primary hypothyroidism is typically characterized by:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Failure of the thyroid gland reduces T₄ secretion, resulting in compensatory elevation of TSH.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 37) Primary hyperthyroidism is most commonly associated with:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Excess thyroid hormone suppresses pituitary TSH secretion through negative feedback.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 38) The hormone that increases serum calcium concentration is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Parathyroid hormone raises serum calcium by acting on bone, kidneys and indirectly on the intestine.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 39) Calcitonin is secreted by:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Calcitonin lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 40) The principal hormone regulating long-term calcium homeostasis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Parathyroid hormone is the major regulator of extracellular calcium concentration.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 41) The active form of vitamin D is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Calcitriol is the biologically active form of vitamin D that promotes intestinal calcium absorption.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 42) Which endocrine gland secretes cortisol?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Cortisol is produced by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 43) The principal glucocorticoid in humans is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Cortisol regulates glucose metabolism, immune function and the stress response.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 44) The principal mineralocorticoid secreted by the adrenal cortex is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium balance by acting on the distal nephron.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 45) Which hormone is secreted by the adrenal medulla?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines, mainly adrenaline and noradrenaline.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 46) ACTH is secreted by the:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce glucocorticoids.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 47) The hormone that stimulates cortisol secretion is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: ACTH from the anterior pituitary regulates cortisol secretion through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 48) A patient presents with weight gain, hypertension, purple striae and hyperglycemia. The most likely endocrine disorder is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Excess cortisol causes central obesity, hypertension, hyperglycemia, proximal muscle weakness and characteristic purple striae.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 49) A patient with fatigue, hypotension, hyperpigmentation and hyponatremia most likely has:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes cortisol and aldosterone deficiency with increased ACTH, producing hyperpigmentation.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 50) A patient presents with episodic headache, palpitations and sweating associated with severe hypertension. The most likely diagnosis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumor causing paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 51) Growth hormone is secreted by the:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Growth hormone (GH) is synthesized and secreted by somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 52) The major mediator of growth hormone action is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Most growth-promoting effects of GH are mediated through insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), produced mainly by the liver.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 53) Excess growth hormone secretion before epiphyseal closure causes:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Excess GH before closure of the growth plates results in excessive linear growth.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 54) Excess growth hormone secretion after epiphyseal closure causes:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Acromegaly is characterized by enlargement of the hands, feet and facial bones after skeletal maturity.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 55) Prolactin secretion is physiologically inhibited by:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Dopamine from the hypothalamus exerts tonic inhibition on prolactin secretion.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 56) The posterior pituitary releases:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: ADH and oxytocin are synthesized in the hypothalamus and stored and released from the posterior pituitary.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 57) The hormone primarily responsible for uterine contraction during labor is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Oxytocin stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction and facilitates childbirth.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 58) The principal physiological action of prolactin is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Prolactin stimulates development of the mammary glands and milk synthesis after delivery.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 59) The hormone that stimulates thyroid hormone synthesis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: TSH binds to thyroid follicular cells and promotes synthesis and secretion of T₃ and T₄.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 60) A patient presents with fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain and dry skin. The most likely diagnosis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Reduced thyroid hormone levels decrease metabolic activity, producing fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 61) A young woman presents with weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor and diffuse goiter. The most likely diagnosis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism and is characterized by diffuse toxic goiter.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 62) The biochemical hallmark of primary hyperparathyroidism is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Excess parathyroid hormone increases serum calcium while promoting renal phosphate excretion.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 63) Which biochemical finding is most characteristic of primary adrenal insufficiency?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Aldosterone deficiency causes sodium loss and potassium retention.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 64) The screening test of choice for Cushing syndrome is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Failure of cortisol suppression after low-dose dexamethasone suggests Cushing syndrome.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 65) A patient with resistant hypertension and persistent hypokalemia is most likely to have:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Excess aldosterone causes sodium retention, hypertension and increased renal potassium loss.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 66) The most sensitive biochemical test for pheochromocytoma is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Plasma free metanephrines have high sensitivity for detecting catecholamine-secreting tumors.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 67) A patient with polyuria, polydipsia and low urine osmolality despite hypernatremia most likely has:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Diabetes insipidus results from ADH deficiency or resistance, producing dilute urine despite dehydration.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 68) Which hormone primarily regulates serum phosphate along with calcium?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: PTH decreases renal phosphate reabsorption while increasing serum calcium.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 69) The principal action of calcitriol is to:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Calcitriol enhances intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 70) A patient presents with recurrent renal stones, bone pain and elevated serum calcium. The most likely diagnosis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Hypercalcemia, nephrolithiasis and bone disease are classic manifestations of primary hyperparathyroidism.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 71) A patient with diabetes mellitus has persistent HbA1c of 9.5%. This primarily indicates:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: HbA1c reflects the average blood glucose over the preceding 2–3 months; values above target indicate inadequate control.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 72) The first biochemical abnormality in diabetic nephropathy is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Microalbuminuria is the earliest detectable marker of diabetic kidney damage before overt proteinuria develops.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 73) A patient presents with fasting hypoglycemia, elevated serum insulin and elevated C-peptide levels. The most likely diagnosis is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Endogenous insulin secretion increases both insulin and C-peptide concentrations, unlike exogenous insulin administration.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 74) A patient receiving exogenous insulin develops hypoglycemia. Which laboratory finding helps distinguish this from insulinoma?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Pharmaceutical insulin does not contain C-peptide, so endogenous C-peptide levels remain suppressed.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 75) A patient with chronic alcohol use presents with recurrent fasting hypoglycemia after prolonged fasting. The most likely mechanism is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Alcohol metabolism increases the NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, inhibiting gluconeogenesis and predisposing to fasting hypoglycemia.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 76) The most abundant protein in human plasma is:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Albumin constitutes about 60% of plasma proteins and maintains plasma oncotic pressure while transporting various substances.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 77) Which plasma protein is primarily responsible for iron transport?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Transferrin binds ferric iron in plasma and delivers it to tissues, especially the bone marrow.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 78) Ceruloplasmin primarily transports:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Ceruloplasmin is the major copper-carrying protein in plasma and also has ferroxidase activity.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 79) A patient with nephrotic syndrome is most likely to have:
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Heavy urinary protein loss causes hypoalbuminemia, leading to edema due to reduced plasma oncotic pressure.

Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.question: 80) A patient with obstructive jaundice has elevated bilirubin, ALP and GGT. Which additional finding is most likely?
Clinical Biochemistry & Endocrinology.exp: Obstruction prevents bile pigments from reaching the intestine, producing pale stools and dark urine.
